6bbc0c96eb:
This chapter walks through a complete repository that turns official sample question 3 into running code. There is one inventory integration, built once as an MCP server. Claude Code uses it through a committed .mcp.json. So does a multi-agent restock planner that you write yourself.

The planner is a coordinator with three kinds of subagents: demand analysis, supplier terms and purchase-order drafting. Each runs in its own context with an explicit brief. They run in parallel, code audits what they return, and a human approval gate stands in front of the only write.
bf8827526a: Prerequisites: chapter 22 (MCP server development) for the protocol; chapter 21 (tool implementation) for tool design and is_error; chapters 01 to 03 (agent architecture, construction, patterns) for loops and subagents; chapter 20 for hooks and secrets. The repository produced every trace and number in this chapter when the chapter was built. Nothing is hand-typed output.
8179747bf2:
When several applications need the same backend, you wrap it once as an MCP server that describes its own tools, resources and prompts, and every MCP-capable host (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, your own agent) discovers and uses it through the same protocol, instead of each application carrying a private copy of the integration.

On top of that server, a coordinator splits restock planning into narrow subagents that each see only their brief and only the tools they need, verifies everything they return against the server's own records, and lets a human approve each purchase order before code (never a model) calls the one tool that spends money, with an idempotency key so a retry can never order twice.
69b9c54661:
Most of the exam's Domain 8, and a good part of Domains 1, 6 and 7, can be asked as questions about this one system:

  • Which integration mechanism: custom tool, REST call in the app, or MCP server?
  • Where does the approval check live: prompt, tool description, or harness code?
  • What does a subagent know when it starts: everything the coordinator saw, or only its brief?
  • What should a tool return when the supplier portal times out: an exception, an empty list, or a structured error with a retry hint?
  • What happens when a network timeout makes the client retry a write?

The repository answers each one in code, and the tests prove the answers hold. Read the chapter with the repository open. Every code block below is cut from the real files when the chapter is built, so the text cannot drift from the code.
fde590477e:
A regional retailer runs three distribution centres: Newark (NJ1), Dallas (TX2) and Ontario, California (CA3). Its inventory lives in two systems that don't always agree.

The first is a warehouse management system (WMS). It counts what is physically on the shelves, and it is the system of record. The second is an ERP. It keeps its own on-hand figure from receipts and shipments, and that figure drifts when a feed is late.

A supplier portal provides lead times, pack sizes, unit costs and minimum order values. It times out often enough that everyone on the buying team has a story about it. Purchase orders are placed through the ERP.
2d06e9fcdf:
Three groups want Claude to work with this data. Developers on the supply-chain team use Claude Code. While they build reports, they want to ask "which SKUs at NJ1 are under ten days of cover". Buyers use Claude Desktop and want to look up a supplier's terms in the middle of a negotiation.

The planning team wants a nightly restock planner. It looks at every SKU in a warehouse and works out what to order from whom. Then it puts a short packet in front of a buyer, who approves or rejects each order in the morning.

That third consumer is the one we build in full. The first two get the server through configuration only, which is the whole point of choosing MCP.
c7e87d5e43:
Before writing code, write down what "done" means, because those statements become the tests. The functional requirements are short:

  • find SKUs whose days of cover fall below the horizon plus the supplier's lead time;
  • size an order in whole packs that brings cover back to the horizon;
  • respect each supplier's minimum order value;
  • produce one purchase order per supplier per warehouse;
  • put every proposed order in front of a named human;
  • create only what that human approved.

The non-functional requirements are where the design decisions come from:
ca4741e28d:
Notice that only one row is about the model being clever. Everything else is about what must be true no matter what the model does. That ratio is typical of production agent systems, and of the exam's preferred answers. The model makes the judgement calls. Code makes the guarantees.

Watch for answer options that move a guarantee into a prompt ("instruct the agent never to create a purchase order without approval"). That's the distractor. A prompt changes the probability of a behaviour; a check in code changes the possibility.
0c36c874bc:
There are three reasonable ways to let Claude use the inventory system, and the exam expects you to know when each one wins.

The first is to call the REST API directly from application code and paste the results into the prompt. The application decides what to fetch. The model never chooses.

The second is a custom tool. You write a tool definition (name, description, JSON schema) in your application and pass it in the tools array of a Messages API request. When the model emits a tool_use block, your code calls the REST API and returns a tool_result.

The third is an MCP server. This is a separate program that wraps the REST API and exposes tools, resources and prompts through the Model Context Protocol. Any MCP host can connect to it and discover what it offers.
e5f1ca3c51:
For a single application with one or two tools, a custom tool is the simplest correct answer. There's no extra process, no protocol and no deployment. The tool code sits next to the loop that calls it.

The trouble starts when the second and third applications arrive. Each one needs the same tool definitions, argument validation, error mapping, retry rules and credentials handling. Each team copies the code, then changes its copy. Six months later the Claude Code helper returns days_of_cover as a string. The planner's copy still has the old warehouse list. And nobody can say which version of "conflict" the Desktop users are seeing.

This is the N x M problem from chapter 22: N clients times M systems, each pair with its own adapter.
451cedf80b:
An MCP server collapses that to one implementation per backend. The server owns the tool names, descriptions, schemas, validation, error categories and credentials. The hosts own the model, the conversation and the approvals.

Claude Code reads a .mcp.json committed to the repository and starts the server. Claude Desktop reads its own config file and starts the same server. The restock planner reads the same .mcp.json and starts the same server again.

Say the inventory team adds a field or tightens a description. All three consumers see it on the next connection, because tools are discovered at connection time rather than compiled into each client. That's what official sample question 3 is testing: a reusable integration across several applications points to MCP.
b74d3556fc: The decision is not "MCP always". The table below is the version to memorise, with the reason for each row. The exam phrases these as a scenario, with one or two details that tip the answer.
4a17e4a36a:
Two finer points belong here, because they come up in questions.

First, MCP does not make a tool more capable. The planner turns each MCP tool into an ordinary Messages API tool (name, description, input schema) before the model sees it. So the model's behaviour depends on the same things as for a custom tool, chiefly the description.

Second, MCP is not a security boundary by itself. The server runs with whatever credentials you give it, and the host decides which of its tools a given agent may call. In this repository both controls are explicit. The server is the only holder of the database path (and in production would be the only holder of the ERP credentials). The planner's bridge filters tools per agent and refuses the write without an approval.
9d392d3730:
Why stdio and not HTTP? The transport follows from where the clients run. All three consumers in this scenario run on the same machine as the server when they use it: a developer's laptop, a buyer's desktop, the planning job's host. So stdio is the simplest choice. The host starts the server as a child process, and the server inherits only the environment variables the host passes. There's no port, no TLS and no token to manage.

Suppose the planner moved to a cluster and the Desktop users sat in another building. Then you'd put the same tool code behind the Streamable HTTP transport with OAuth (chapter 22 sections 09 and 16). The tool functions would not change. Keeping the domain logic in store.py, away from the protocol, is what makes that move cheap.
68c57cc3eb:
A single agent could do the whole job. Give one Sonnet conversation the four inventory tools and the prompt "plan a restock for NJ1". A good model will call get_stock nine times and get_supplier four times, do the arithmetic, and write a plan.

For one small warehouse that's a reasonable design. The repository even ships the MCP prompt restock_review for exactly that single-agent use from Claude Code or Desktop. So the question isn't whether subagents are possible. It's what they buy here that is worth their cost. There are four answers, and one counter-argument.
a1fd53a78b:
Context isolation. Each get_stock result is about 120 tokens of JSON. A real catalog has thousands of SKUs per warehouse, each with readings from two systems and a sales history.

A single agent accumulates every one of those results in its conversation. Every later turn pays for all of them again as input tokens. Meanwhile the details it needs for the order (nine numbers per candidate SKU) are buried among hundreds of results that turned out to be fine. Chapter 03's context-rot discussion applies directly: accuracy on the specific numbers falls as the context fills with similar-looking data.

A demand subagent reads its shard of results, keeps what matters, and hands back a structured report. The coordinator never holds raw tool output at all.
88556a811d:
Least privilege per role. The demand analyst needs get_stock and nothing else. The supplier analyst needs get_supplier. The PO drafter needs no inventory tools at all, because everything it needs is in its brief. Nobody but the coordinator's code gets create_purchase_order.

A single agent must hold every tool the whole job needs, including the write, for the whole run. Any text it reads is read by an agent that can spend money. That includes a supplier note field, or an item description that someone pasted instructions into. With subagents, a prompt injection that reaches the demand analyst can at worst make it call get_stock with odd arguments.
709354cc0a:
Parallelism. The four demand shards and the supplier lookup don't depend on each other, so they run at the same time. The three drafters also run at the same time.

The fake-model run adds an artificial 0.4 second latency per model call. With it, phase 1 finishes in about 0.8 seconds (two model turns), not the 4 seconds that five agents in sequence would take. With real models, where a turn takes seconds, that difference is minutes per warehouse per night.
9f6df736c0:
Model mix. Looking up stock and copying numbers into a schema is a job for the smallest model. Drafting an order with arithmetic and a rationale benefits from a stronger one. Subagents let you choose per role.

In the measured run below, the five Haiku 5.5 agents consumed about three quarters of all input tokens and cost about 15% of the total. The same phase-1 traffic on Sonnet 5.5 would have cost roughly twenty times as much.
b6eff7490f:
The counter-argument is overhead and coordination risk. Every subagent repeats a system prompt and tool definitions. Every brief must carry exactly the facts the subagent needs; forget one, and the subagent cannot know it. And every report must be merged.

The exam's official sample on a research system names "overly narrow decomposition by the coordinator" as a root cause of poor results. If the coordinator splits the work so that no subagent sees what it needs, the answer is wrong however good each subagent is.

This design defends against that in three ways. The data fixes the decomposition: one demand shard per supplier, because orders are per supplier. Code builds the briefs from the catalog. And the coordinator checks that every expected SKU came back.
c3f86e7275: The table summarises the four roles. The column that matters most for the exam is "tools". Each role has the smallest set that lets it do its job, and the only write is outside every model's reach.
b0a7ca1b53:
The third decision is the one that makes the system safe to run unattended. Draw a line between the parts that must always be right and the parts that may be usually right. Then put the first group in code.

The model is good at reading semi-structured results, deciding which tool to call next, explaining a number in a sentence, and writing a summary a buyer will read. Code is good at arithmetic, comparing two values, refusing a call, and remembering who approved what. Each responsibility in the planner sits on one side of the line on purpose.
99aefcc5e8:
Two consequences follow, and both are exam themes.

First, a model output is never trusted just because it is well-formed. The PO drafter returns schema-valid JSON every time (the loop rejects anything else). Yet the coordinator still recomputes every quantity. A schema guarantees shape. It says nothing about whether 216 or 240 is the right number of water bottles. Chapter 21 calls this skepticism of confident output; in this repository it's a function called _accept_draft.

Second, the model gets work only where its judgement adds something. You may fairly ask why the drafter exists at all if code recomputes the quantities. In this capstone the formula is simple on purpose, so the checks are easy to read. The drafter's real value is the rationale line the buyer reads and the notes it adds about borderline cases. In a real system it would also weigh things the formula cannot, like a promotion next week or a supplier's recent short shipments.

The pattern holds either way: the model proposes, code verifies, a human approves, code executes.
8856e540de:
The repository has two halves that mirror the two halves of the design. inventory_mcp/ is the server: protocol, domain store, tool definitions. planner/ is the host: coordinator, subagent loop, bridge to MCP, cost ledger, model client.

Nothing in inventory_mcp/ imports from planner/. The server knows nothing about agents, which is what lets Claude Code use it unchanged. The planner imports exactly two things from the server package: the stdio client and the JSON Schema validator, both from protocol.py. They play the role the official SDK's client classes play in a real build.
afafc932d2:
Three details make the runs reproducible, and each is a habit worth copying.

  • The store fixes "today" at 2026-10-09. It generates 28 days of sales from a weekly pattern that sums to zero, so the average daily sales are exact integers and you can check every number in this chapter by hand.
  • Each planner run uses a fresh temporary SQLite file unless you pass --db, so runs don't interfere.
  • The fake model is deterministic. Given the same request it returns the same blocks, so the token counts, the cost table and the traces below are identical on every machine.
e53f17912a:
The protocol layer is a small, dependency-free implementation of the parts of MCP the capstone needs. It's adapted from the chapter 22 companion's mcplite.py. It is written out in full, rather than taken from the official mcp package, for two reasons. You can read every message the server sends. And the tests run anywhere with only the standard library.

In a production build you would use the official SDK (FastMCP-style decorators in the Python SDK; check the docs for the current class names). The tool functions in server.py would move across almost unchanged, because they are plain functions with type hints and docstrings.
f9d7d21034: On stdio, MCP messages are JSON-RPC 2.0 objects, one per line, UTF-8, with no embedded newlines. The host writes requests to the server's stdin and reads responses from its stdout. Everything the server wants to log must go to stderr. A single stray print() on stdout is a line the client tries to parse as JSON-RPC. So the transport loop is short and strict:
9ff13cb513:
Three rules are visible in those lines.

A line that isn't JSON gets a JSON-RPC parse error (-32700) with a null id, and the loop continues. One bad line must not kill a server that other requests depend on.

A notification (a message with no id) gets no response at all. That's why handle can return None.

And the server exits when stdin closes. This is the first step of the spec's stdio shutdown sequence: the client closes stdin, waits, then sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL. The contract test test_clean_shutdown_on_stdin_close checks that the process exits with status 0 at the first step.
9bc09f6c94:
The dispatcher implements the lifecycle. Under the protocol revisions up to 2025-11-25, it runs in three steps:

  1. The client sends initialize with the protocol version it wants, its capabilities and its name.
  2. The server answers with the version it will speak (the same one if it supports it, otherwise its own latest), its capabilities, its name and optional instructions.
  3. The client sends the notifications/initialized notification, and normal operation begins.

Any other request before initialize is refused, except ping.

The newer stateless style (revision 2026-07-28, covered in chapter 22) drops the handshake. Instead, every request carries the protocol version and client capabilities in _meta, and server/discover handles capability discovery. The server supports both, and the contract tests exercise both. Version details move quickly, so check the current specification before relying on either.
8e9ddca2f0:
The routing table maps each method to the capability that must be advertised for it. A method whose capability the server did not advertise is "method not found" (-32601), even if the code for it exists.

That matters for the contract. A client is entitled to assume that a server without a prompts capability won't answer prompts/list. A test that only checks the happy path would never notice a server that answers methods it never advertised.
377547abb0:
Each tool is a Python function registered with a decorator. The decorator builds the MCP tool definition from the function:

  • the docstring text before Args: becomes the description;
  • each Args: line becomes a parameter description;
  • the type hints become JSON Schema types;
  • defaults make a parameter optional;
  • a constraints dictionary adds patterns, enums and ranges.

This is the same convention FastMCP uses, and it has one large benefit. The schema cannot drift from the function signature, because it is generated from it.
aa78310df7:
Read the two descriptions as the model will. Tool descriptions are the main signal a model uses to choose a tool and fill its arguments (chapter 21). So each one says what the tool is for, and when to use it instead of its neighbour ("if you already know the SKU, call get_stock directly"). It says what comes back. And it says what an edge case means ("an empty list means no match, not an error"; "conflict=true means ... do not plan an order on that number").

The get_stock description even states the days-of-cover formula. A model that sees days_of_cover: 7.5 then knows it already includes stock on order. A vague description such as "Gets stock" would leave the model to guess all of that, and the guesses would differ between Haiku and Sonnet.
648aee623a:
The schemas do work that descriptions cannot. sku has the pattern ^SKU-\d{4}$, and the warehouse is an enum. The PO's lines array needs at least one item, each with an integer qty between 1 and 100,000. Every object schema sets additionalProperties: false.

The server validates every tools/call against the schema before the function runs. So a model that sends "sku": "1001" gets a validation error that names the pattern, not a confusing "not found".

The model receives the same schema as input_schema in its tool definition, so a well-behaved model rarely trips the check. But the server can't assume its clients are well-behaved. Claude Code, a script and a future client all call the same server.
a9cf536b6e:
The write tool carries three design choices.

Its description says it spends money and must only be called after a human has approved "this exact order". That helps a model in Claude Code behave. It is not the control; section 16 shows the control.

Its idempotency_key is required, not optional. A write tool whose retries can duplicate effects should make the safe path the only path.

Its annotations say readOnlyHint: false, destructiveHint: false (it creates; it doesn't delete or overwrite), idempotentHint: true and openWorldHint: true (it reaches an external system). Annotations are hints from the server to the host, used for things like deciding which tools need a confirmation prompt. The MCP specification says clients must not rely on them for security decisions when the server is untrusted. So the planner's gate doesn't read them at all.
bc209e47e0:
MCP has two error channels, and putting a failure in the wrong one is a common exam distractor.

A protocol error is a JSON-RPC error object instead of a result. The request itself was wrong: unknown method, unknown tool, malformed params, unknown resource. The host usually handles it in code, and the model may never see it.

A tool execution error is a normal result with isError: true. The request was well-formed and the tool ran, but the operation failed for a reason the model can act on: bad argument value, item not found, supplier unavailable, business rule. The host passes it to the model as a tool_result with is_error: true, and the model decides what to do next.
a2ae881547:
Inside the isError channel, a bare message such as "Error" or "Operation failed" gives the model nothing to decide with. Every error from this server carries a structured payload with four fixed fields:

  • errorCategory: validation, not_found, business, permission, transient or internal;
  • isRetryable;
  • a message for humans and models;
  • a hint that says what to do next.

Category-specific details ride along: retry_after_ms for transient errors, existing_po_id when an idempotency key is reused, order_value and min_order_value when a PO is too small.

The payload appears twice in the result. It's JSON text in content, which is what most hosts show the model. It's also structuredContent, which is what code reads. That follows the spec's advice to keep a text rendering for clients that don't use structured content.
d0fa9792ca:
Look at the order of the branches.

  • An unknown tool name is a protocol error (-32602). No tool ran, and the model can't fix it by changing argument values; the host should never have offered a tool the server doesn't have.
  • Arguments that fail the schema become an isError result with category validation, because the model can fix them.
  • A ToolError raised by the domain code passes through with its own category.
  • Any other exception becomes a generic internal error whose message says nothing about the cause.

In that last case the traceback goes to stderr, where operators can see it. It doesn't go to the model, where it would leak implementation details into a conversation that might be shown to a user. The contract test test_internal_crash_is_generic_iserror replaces get_stock with a function that divides by zero. It then asserts that "ZeroDivision" appears nowhere in the result.
e8570d1829:
The difference between "access failed" and "valid empty result" deserves its own paragraph, because the exam tests it directly.

search_items with a query that matches nothing returns {"count": 0, "items": []} with isError: false. get_stock for a SKU the warehouse doesn't carry returns warehouses: [], also a success. If either returned an error, a model would retry or report a fault where there is none.

The reverse mistake is worse. If get_supplier returned an empty object on a timeout instead of a transient error, a model would conclude the supplier has no items, and an agent would plan on that. The repository has a test for each side of that line.
ffd645497c:
Tools are model-controlled: the model decides when to call them. Resources are application-controlled: the host decides when to read them and what to do with the content.

This server exposes two. inventory://catalog lists every SKU with its name, category, supplier and pack size, plus the supplier list with status. inventory://warehouses lists the valid warehouse codes. Both are reference data that every planning run needs. Without them you'd pay for a chain of exploratory tool calls: "search everything", "search page two", "which warehouses exist?".
e70c267cb6:
The planner's coordinator reads both resources in phase 0, in code, before any model call. It uses them for three things:

  • rejecting an unknown warehouse before spending a token (the test test_unknown_warehouse_rejected_before_any_model_call asserts zero model calls);
  • building the decomposition, with SKUs grouped by supplier;
  • checking the subagents' reports: every expected SKU must come back, and pack sizes and supplier IDs must match the catalog.

In Claude Code, the user can attach the same resources to a conversation (check the docs for the current mention syntax). That gives a developer the catalog in context without a single tool call.

An unknown resource URI is a protocol error (-32602) with the URI in data. Returning empty contents would look like an empty catalog.
07a9a51a17:
The prompt restock_review is the third primitive, and it's user-controlled. A person picks it from a menu and fills its arguments, and the host inserts the resulting messages into the conversation. Claude Code surfaces MCP prompts as slash commands (check the docs for the exact naming format).

This prompt packages the single-agent version of the restock workflow. It's for buyers and developers who want an interactive review rather than the nightly planner. It ends with an explicit instruction not to call create_purchase_order but to present drafts for approval. That instruction is guidance for an interactive session, where a human watches every tool call. The planner doesn't rely on it.
7b007586a5:
The server also sends instructions in its initialize result. This short paragraph tells any host what the server is for and which resource to read first. It says the WMS is the system of record, and that the write tool needs a human approver and a stable idempotency key.

Hosts may add server instructions to the model's context (Claude Code does, subject to its own limits; check the docs). Keep them short and factual. They're read on every session.
e7729faead:
store.py holds the domain rules and nothing else. It's plain functions over a sqlite3 connection, which raise ToolError with a category when a rule is broken. The MCP layer wraps them. The store tests call them directly, without a server, the same way you'd unit-test a Spring @Service without starting the web layer.

Two rules in it carry most of the capstone's failure handling: how stock readings from two systems are reconciled, and how a purchase order is created exactly once.
e14eecd642:
Conflicting stock data. The stock_readings table keeps one row per SKU, warehouse and source (wms or erp). get_stock always reports the WMS figure as on_hand and says so ("system_of_record": "wms"). It lists every reading with its source and timestamp.

It sets conflict: true when the readings differ by more than 5 units and more than 10% of the larger value. Both thresholds are needed. A gap of 5 units on a slow item selling 2 a day is meaningful. A 4-unit gap on a pallet of 900 cables is counting noise.

The tool doesn't pick a winner, average the readings, or hide the disagreement. It reports provenance (which system said what, and when) and leaves the decision to the caller. Its description tells the model what the caller should do: report it, and don't plan an order on that number. Section 20 shows the drill.
7c3ab36edb:
The idempotent write. Networks fail in the worst place: after the server has committed the purchase order, and before the client has read the response. The client sees a timeout and can't tell whether the PO exists. If it retries a plain "create" call, the supplier gets two orders.

The standard fix is an idempotency key; payment APIs use it for the same reason. The client generates a key for the operation and sends it with every attempt. The server stores the key with the result of the first successful attempt. A repeat with the same key returns the stored result instead of acting again.
7347378e0a:
Two refinements make the key safe rather than merely convenient.

First, the server stores a hash of the request content alongside the key: supplier, warehouse, and the sorted list of SKU and quantity pairs. A repeat with the same key and the same content is a retry, and gets the original PO back with replayed: true. A repeat with the same key and different content is a bug upstream: two different orders sharing a key. The server refuses it with a business error that names the existing PO. It won't silently return a PO that doesn't match what the caller asked for.

Second, the key column has a UNIQUE constraint, so even two concurrent first attempts can't both insert.

Line order doesn't matter to the hash, and a test checks this. A client that rebuilds the same order may list lines differently.
79b3bbb2ef:
Where the key comes from matters as much as the server rule. A random UUID generated at call time defeats the purpose. If the planner crashes after the PO is created and is restarted, the restarted run generates a new UUID and orders again.

So the planner derives the key from the order's content and the planning date: rst-2026-10-09-NJ1-SUP-ACME- plus ten hex characters of a hash of the sorted lines. A restarted run on the same day that produces the same order produces the same key, and the server replays. A different order (different quantities after new stock arrived) produces a different key and becomes a new PO, which is correct.

Section 20's duplicate-PO drill runs the whole planner twice against the same database. It shows three POs, not six.
b8b777b89d:
Claude Code reads project-scope MCP servers from a .mcp.json file at the repository root. That file is meant to be committed, so the whole team gets the same servers. Personal servers go in the user or local scope instead (chapter 22 section 17).

The file names the server, its transport, the command that starts it, and the environment it receives. Claude Code expands ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} inside it. That's what lets a committed file refer to machine-specific paths and secrets without containing them (check the docs for the full list of fields that support expansion).
257e372794:
Each expansion is there for a reason.

  • ${PYTHON:-python3} lets a developer with a virtualenv point at its interpreter without editing the file.
  • ${INVENTORY_REPO:-.} resolves the launcher relative to the project directory by default.
  • ${INVENTORY_DB:-data/inventory.db} gives every developer a local database by default, and lets CI or the nightly job point at another.
  • ${INVENTORY_FAULTS:-} defaults to empty, so drills are opt-in.

In a production version the env block would also carry "ERP_TOKEN": "${ERP_TOKEN}" with no default. The committed file holds the reference, and each machine holds the value. A missing value is then an error at startup, not a confusing failure at the first tool call.
761e8c515a:
The planner reads the same file. planner/mcp_config.py re-implements the expansion rule and adds two host-provided defaults: the current interpreter and the repository path. Then it spawns the server with the expanded command and environment.

Using one file for both hosts is the configuration-management point of the capstone. There's one definition of how the inventory server starts, reviewed in one pull request. The nightly job can't drift from what developers test against.
36b59e3787:
The expansion is strict by default. A variable with no value and no default raises MissingVariable when the config is loaded.

Failing at startup is the right behaviour for a credential. A server that starts with an empty token fails later, inside a tool call, with an authentication error that the model then tries to explain to a user.

The tests check five things:

  • defaults apply;
  • environment values win over defaults;
  • a missing variable fails fast;
  • the committed file contains references and no absolute paths;
  • a relative database path resolves against the repository, not whatever directory the host happened to start in.
6ed6f095b0: scripts/wire_trace.py starts the server from .mcp.json with the supplier-outage fault turned on. It runs a short session and prints every JSON-RPC message in both directions. The output below is that script's real output, cut at 230 characters per line. Read it once from top to bottom. Nearly every MCP mechanism in the exam guide appears in it.
6fb2a04f60:
Line by line. The client opens with initialize (id 1), naming protocol version 2025-11-25 and empty capabilities. The server answers with the same version and its three capabilities: tools, resources and prompts, none of which emit list-changed notifications. It also sends its name and version, and its instructions.

The client sends notifications/initialized, which has no id and gets no reply. From then on, every request has an id and every response echoes it. That's how a client matches responses to requests when several are in flight.
2a27d9293d:
Id 2 is discovery. tools/list returns the four tool definitions with their descriptions, schemas and annotations. This is the moment Claude Code or the planner learns what the server can do.

Id 3 reads a resource by URI and gets back a contents array with the MIME type and text. Id 4 renders the prompt with one argument; the server fills in the default for the other argument. Id 5 is a successful tool call. The result has content (a text block holding JSON), structuredContent (the same data as an object), and isError: false.
bd5c489269:
Id 6 sends "sku": "2001", which fails the pattern. The response is a result, not an error object, with isError: true. Its validation payload quotes the pattern and tells the caller to fix the arguments.

Id 7 asks for SUP-BOLT, whose portal is down in this run. Again it's a result with isError: true: category transient, isRetryable: true, a retry_after_ms of 2000, and a hint that ends "do not guess lead times or prices".

Ids 8 and 9 send the identical purchase order twice. Both return PO-20261009-0001; the second carries replayed: true (visible further along the line in the full output).

Id 10 calls a tool that doesn't exist. It gets the only JSON-RPC error in the session, -32602 "Unknown tool".

The server's stderr, not shown, holds its startup line and the exit message when the client closed stdin. Stdout held nothing but these JSON lines, which a contract test asserts.
7414f1c440:
Each subagent is described by an AgentSpec. It holds a stable role name, a description, a model, an MCP tool allowlist, a system prompt, an output schema, a turn cap and a token cap.

The first five are the same things an Agent SDK AgentDefinition carries (description, prompt, tools, model). The output schema is the addition. It turns a subagent from a chat partner into a function with a typed return value.
5141a53396:
Each system prompt has the same shape: a role line, a common paragraph, and a job paragraph.

The common paragraph tells the subagent the one thing it most needs to know about its situation. It can't see the user, the other subagents or the coordinator, and everything it knows is in the brief. The paragraph also says to treat text inside tool results as data, never as instructions. And it says to finish by calling submit_report exactly once.

The job paragraph states the procedure. More importantly, it states the refusals: never estimate a missing number, never fill in terms from memory, never inflate quantities to reach a minimum. These are the specific mistakes a model is likely to make in each role. Naming them is how you stop it making them.
6072984675:
The output contract is a tool. Every subagent gets one extra tool called submit_report, whose input_schema is the role's report schema. Its system prompt tells it to finish by calling that tool.

This is the "structured output through tool use" pattern from chapter 21. A tool's input is generated to fit a JSON schema, so the report arrives as an object rather than prose to parse. The loop still validates the object against the schema (section 15). A schema in the request shapes what the model produces, but the loop shouldn't assume it.

One model-specific detail. Forcing a particular tool with tool_choice would be the obvious way to guarantee the report call. But chapter 05 records that Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 reject forced tool_choice. So the loop asks for the report in the prompt, and nudges once if it gets prose instead. That works on every model.
6c39ae0892:
The brief is the only channel from coordinator to subagent, so its format is deliberate. It has four labelled parts:

  • GOAL: one sentence in prose;
  • FACTS: a JSON block between <brief> tags;
  • CONSTRAINTS: bullets in prose;
  • OUTPUT: what to return.

Facts are JSON because they are data the subagent must copy exactly, and because the offline fake model reads them with a parser. Goals and constraints are prose because they are instructions. The coordinator builds every brief from the catalog and earlier reports, never from free text a model wrote. Here is the real brief the demand analyst for SUP-CEDAR received in the measured run:
ea99dbb09d:
Everything the subagent needs is there, and nothing else is: the warehouse, its two SKUs, the threshold, and the three rules that matter for this role. It doesn't see the other seven SKUs, the supplier terms, the horizon, the other shards' results, or anything the user or coordinator said.

That's the "subagents do not inherit context; pass it explicitly" principle (chapter 03) in concrete form. A test asserts it: the serialised transcript of the ACME shard must not contain any BOLT SKU or the string SUP-BOLT.
b27d80f057:
The review threshold shows a small decomposition choice. The demand analysts run in parallel with the supplier analyst, so they can't know each supplier's lead time.

The coordinator could serialise the phases: supplier terms first, then demand. It doesn't. It gives demand a generous threshold instead: the horizon plus a 14-day buffer, longer than any supplier's lead time. The drafter applies the exact lead time later. A SKU flagged as a candidate that turns out not to need stock simply produces no line.

The cost of this choice is a few extra candidate rows. The benefit is that the two slowest lookups overlap.
9abca58d59:
run_subagent is the tool-use loop each subagent runs. It's the loop from chapter 02 with three additions:

  • the conversation starts from the brief and nothing else;
  • every MCP tool call goes through the bridge with the subagent's allowlist;
  • the loop ends on a validated submit_report call, not on end_turn or on text that looks finished.
02e1744f65:
Walk through what each branch prevents.

Isolation is structural. messages is a new list whose only element is the brief. So there's no shared history to leak, whatever the coordinator's conversation contains. The tools list is built from the spec's allowlist plus submit_report. A subagent can't even see a tool it isn't allowed to call.

The stop signal is structured. The loop doesn't parse "I'm done" from text, and it doesn't stop on end_turn with a prose answer. It stops when the model calls submit_report with input that validates. If the model answers in prose, the loop asks once, explicitly, for the report. If the report fails validation, the tool result says exactly which fields are wrong, with is_error set. The model then gets another turn to fix them.

The turn cap is a safety net, not the plan. Six turns is three times what a correct run needs. Reaching it is reported as a failure with a reason, never treated as success.

A crash is contained. Any exception (an overloaded API, a bug in a tool wrapper) becomes failure on the result. The coordinator holds that shard's SKUs while the other shards continue. A test makes one shard raise "529 overloaded" and checks that the other suppliers still get proposals.
d1af785bfa:
max_tokens deserves its own line. If a response stops because it hit the token cap, any tool call in it may be truncated. So the loop records a specific failure ("raise max_tokens or narrow the brief"). It won't execute half a call, or ask the model to continue blindly.

Narrowing the brief is usually the better fix. A demand shard with 400 SKUs produces a report that won't fit in 2,000 tokens. That's a decomposition problem, not a token-limit problem.
1ec533dcb8:
This is the complete conversation the subagent had: five messages and two model turns.

On its first turn it issued both get_stock calls at once, as parallel tool-use blocks in one response. The brief asked for that, and it halves the number of turns. On its second turn it classified SKU-3001 as a candidate (6.7 days of cover against a 35-day threshold) and SKU-3002 as ok (40 days), copying the numbers from the tool results.

None of this transcript reaches the coordinator's context. The coordinator receives only the validated report object. It keeps the transcript on the result object for debugging.
f5ab212566: Every MCP call from every agent passes through one object, McpBridge. It's the planner's equivalent of a Claude Code PreToolUse hook, a retry policy and an audit log rolled together. Keeping all three in one place gives you one place to read when you want to know what an agent was allowed to do, and what it did.
5c323d605a: Exposure. tools_for converts MCP tool definitions to Messages API tool definitions, for exactly the tools in an allowlist. It renames each to mcp__inventory__<tool>, the same namespacing Claude Code uses for MCP tools. The namespace prevents a collision between an MCP tool and a local tool of the same name. It also makes it obvious in a transcript which server a call went to.
b78d25f1a5:
The gate. Before any call reaches the server, the bridge checks two things.

A tool outside the caller's allowlist is denied with a permission error and never goes on the wire. A test counts the wire messages before and after to prove it.

And create_purchase_order is denied unless the approval registry holds an approval for exactly that idempotency key, from exactly the person named in approved_by. An approval for one order doesn't approve another. A model can't approve its own order by writing a name into approved_by. Nothing in a prompt or a tool result can add an entry to the registry, because only the coordinator's execute method calls grant, and only for decisions returned by the human approval step.

This is the "prerequisite gate in code, not in the prompt" answer from the official sample questions, applied to spending money.
76f83e00f8:
Local recovery. When the server returns an error marked isRetryable, the bridge waits the server's retry_after_ms (scaled down in tests). It tries once more before handing the result to the model.

So a one-off 503 from the supplier portal is absorbed without costing a model turn. It never appears in the model's context at all. A persistent outage still reaches the model after the second attempt, with the server's category and hint intact. Errors that aren't retryable (validation, not found, business rules) pass through immediately, because retrying them would only repeat the failure.

Retrying writes is safe here only because create_purchase_order is idempotent. Without the key, this retry loop would be the bug.
5293dc0832: Audit. Every call appends an event. It records the caller's label, the tool, the arguments, the error category if any, the number of attempts and the latency, plus the structured result for successes. Section 17 shows the coordinator using these events as the source of truth when it checks what the subagents reported.
3be2eeaa46:
The coordinator's plan method is a fixed pipeline with two parallel phases. It is written as ordinary code, not as a model that decides which subagents to spawn. That's deliberate. The shape of this task is known in advance: look up demand, look up suppliers, draft per supplier. A deterministic workflow is cheaper, faster and easier to test than an agent that rediscovers the same plan every night.

Chapter 01 draws this line between workflows and agents. The subagents are agents, since they choose their tool calls. The coordinator is a workflow that orchestrates them. If the job were open-ended ("investigate why NJ1 keeps running out of chargers"), a model-driven coordinator that chooses its next delegation would fit better.
28c0aaf670:
Fan-out. _parallel submits a list of zero-argument callables to a thread pool. It returns the results in submission order, so results line up with the decomposition no matter which subagent finishes first.

Threads are enough here, because every subagent spends nearly all its time waiting on network I/O: the model API and the MCP server. The stdio client serialises its request and response pairs with a lock. That keeps concurrent calls from interleaving on the one pipe, while the model calls (the slow part) overlap fully. With the async SDK client you'd use asyncio.gather instead; the shape is the same.
83d7f28733:
Aggregation with checks. Phase-1 reports aren't merged as they arrive. Each passes through an acceptance function first. Anything that fails a check becomes a held item with a reason, never a silent drop.

_accept_demand is the most interesting one, because it doesn't trust the numbers the subagent copied. It looks up, in the bridge's audit events, what get_stock actually returned to that subagent for that SKU. Then it compares on_hand, on_order and the sales average with the reported values.
57ccaba92c:
Each check in that function matches a specific way a model can be wrong while producing perfectly valid JSON:

  • A SKU missing from the report (the model skipped one) is held.
  • A row with numbers but no successful get_stock behind it is held. Here the model filled in numbers after a failed call; the demand_invents quirk drill shows this.
  • Numbers that differ from the tool result (a transposed digit, a rounded average) are held, with both values in the reason.
  • A conflict flag that the model failed to report is held anyway, because the coordinator reads the flag from the tool result itself.
  • A pack size or supplier that disagrees with the catalog resource is held.

This is the provenance idea from chapter 03 (keep the link between a claim and its source) turned into code. The coordinator can afford to check because the bridge recorded every source.
539d7dad85:
_accept_suppliers applies the same rule to supplier terms. Then it replaces the reported item prices with the ones from the tool result. The drafter's brief and the final totals are computed from the record, not from a copy.

_accept_draft recomputes every line with the same need_qty function the system prompt describes. It rejects lines for SKUs that weren't candidates, and drafts that dropped a candidate with real need. It recomputes the total from unit costs. And it holds the order if the total is below the supplier's minimum, whatever status the drafter claimed.
5ef9c01dda:
Planning never writes. A test asserts that after plan() the purchase_orders table is empty, and that no event in the bridge's log names create_purchase_order.

Writing happens only in execute(plan, decisions). Here decisions maps each proposal's idempotency key to the name of the person who approved it, or to nothing. The CLI fills decisions by asking at the terminal, showing every line with its quantity, unit cost and rationale. If stdin isn't a terminal and no --approve-as was given, it approves nothing. That's the safe failure for an unattended job that was misconfigured.
2fe357cc2c:
Three steps happen for each approved proposal, in this order.

  1. The approval is recorded in the bridge's registry under the proposal's key and the approver's name. That's what lets the gate open for exactly that call.
  2. Stock is re-read for every line and the quantity recomputed. If anything changed between planning and approval, the proposal is reported as stale and not sent. A delivery may have arrived, the ERP feed may have caught up so the readings now conflict, or sales may have jumped. Planning at 2 a.m. and approving at 9 a.m. leaves a seven-hour gap. A human approving a number that's no longer right is not a safe approval.
  3. Only then is create_purchase_order called, through the bridge, with the plan's content-derived key. The outcome is created, replayed (an earlier attempt already created it) or rejected with the server's structured error.
0446583c1f: Why does code, not the coordinator model, make the call? Because nothing about the call needs judgement. The approved proposal fully determines the arguments. Putting a model between the approval and the write adds a step that can only make things worse, for example by "helpfully" adjusting a quantity the buyer approved. The human approves a specific object. Code submits that object.
2727d4e9f1:
Here is the complete output of python run_planner.py --approve-as "R. Diaz" with the offline fake model, exactly as the repository printed it when this chapter was built.

The first block lists every subagent with its turns, whether it produced a valid report, and the MCP tools it called. An exclamation mark would mark a call that returned isError. Then come the proposals, the held items, the approval-packet summary, the execution outcomes, and the cost ledger.
0a617a26a5:
Check the numbers by hand once. It's the fastest way to trust the system. NJ1 has a horizon of 21 days.

  • SKU-1001 (water bottle, ACME, lead time 5 days, pack 24): 12 a day x (21 + 5) = 312 needed. There are 90 on hand and none on order, so need is 222, rounded up to 10 packs = 240, at 4.10 = 984.00.
  • SKU-1003 (cutting board, pack 10): 3 x 26 = 78, minus 40 on hand and 30 on order = 8. One pack = 10, at 7.25 = 72.50.
  • ACME total: 1,056.50, above its 500 minimum. SKU-1002 has 75 days of cover and is not a candidate.
  • BOLT (lead time 9): SKU-2001 needs 6 x 30 - 50 = 130, so seven packs of 20 = 140, 1,372.00. SKU-2003 needs 2 x 30 - 10 = 50, so five packs of 10, 920.00. Total 2,292.00.
  • CEDAR (lead time 4): SKU-3001 needs 9 x 25 - 60 = 165, so 21 packs of 8 = 168, 873.60.

SKU-4001 (camping lantern) has 6 days of cover. But its supplier, Dune Outdoor, is on hold, so no drafter runs for it, and it is held with that reason.

Eight subagents ran. The drafter for DUNE was never started, because the coordinator knew the supplier status before phase 2.
9aba71df79:
Token costs. The fake client estimates tokens as characters divided by four, over the system prompt, the tool definitions and the messages. The ledger prices them with the guide's lineup: Haiku 5.5 at $0.10 input and $0.50 output per million tokens, Sonnet 5.5 at $2 and $10, Opus 5.5 at $4 and $20. These were verified for this guide on 2026-10-09; check the pricing page before quoting.

Real token counts will be higher. The API adds its own tool-use system prompt, and it counts tokens with the model's tokenizer rather than a character rule (check the docs for the current overhead). But the proportions between agents are what matter for design decisions, and those carry over.
6c9b7a31de:
The design conclusion is in the two columns of that figure. The lookups are where the volume is: 76% of input tokens, because tool results are verbose and each demand shard reads every SKU's readings. Drafting is where the reasoning is, and it's a small amount of text.

Running phase 1 on Sonnet 5.5 instead of Haiku 5.5 would have cost about $0.0238 instead of $0.0012 for the same tokens. That's roughly 20 times as much. On Opus 5.5 it would be about $0.0476.

Per run these are fractions of a cent. But picture three warehouses with ten thousand SKUs each, every night. The token counts grow by three to four orders of magnitude, and the model choice for phase 1 becomes the largest line in the AI budget.

That's the general rule the exam wants. Use the smallest model that does the job reliably for high-volume, low-judgement work. Spend on the larger model where its reasoning changes the outcome.
7e902ec2fb:
Two further levers are not wired in, and both are worth knowing.

Prompt caching would help. Every demand shard sends the same system prompt and the same two tool definitions, which is exactly the stable prefix caching is for. The ledger already records cache_read_input_tokens when a real response reports it. Chapter 15 covers the break-even and minimum cacheable length; check the docs for the current minimum per model.

The Batch API would halve the price of the whole run, if the plan didn't need to be ready at a fixed time. But each subagent here needs several turns with tool results between them, and a batch request can't carry a multi-turn tool loop. You'd have to restructure phase 1 into single-turn requests, with code pre-fetching the stock data. That's a reasonable design for a large overnight job, and it's an exercise at the end of this chapter.
15b929275a:
The server takes an INVENTORY_FAULTS variable that injects specific failures. The fake model takes --quirks, which make one role misbehave in a specific, realistic way. Each drill below is a test in tests/test_planner.py and a line in scripts/run_drills.sh.

Run them before reading the explanations, and predict the output. The point of a drill is to find out whether your mental model of the system matches its behaviour.
4df14fde6b:
--faults supplier_down=SUP-BOLT makes every get_supplier call for Bolt Electronics fail with a transient error after a simulated 5-second timeout. Here is the expected behaviour, layer by layer:

  1. The bridge sees isRetryable: true, waits, and retries once.
  2. The second attempt also fails, so the error goes to the supplier analyst as a tool result with is_error.
  3. The analyst follows its instructions. It reports BOLT as unavailable and copies the error object instead of inventing terms.
  4. The coordinator sees an unavailable supplier and holds BOLT's candidate SKUs, with the error message as the reason.
  5. No drafter is started for BOLT, so no model ever gets a chance to guess Bolt's lead time.

ACME and CEDAR proceed normally.
78d99b5f09:
The exclamation mark in the supplier analyst's tool list marks the failed call. The run degrades rather than fails. Two of three orders go ahead, and the packet tells the buyer exactly which SKUs are waiting on which supplier, and why.

The opposite designs are both wrong, and both appear as exam distractors. Terminating the whole run because one supplier is down throws away good work for the other suppliers. Silently skipping BOLT (or letting the analyst return an empty item list) hides a stock-out risk from the buyer.

The structured error, with a category and a hint, is what makes the middle path possible. The analyst knows the failure is transient and that it must not guess. The coordinator gets a specific reason to show a human.

The flaky variant, supplier_flaky=SUP-BOLT, fails only the first call. There the bridge's single retry succeeds and the analyst sees a clean result. The plan is identical to the normal run. A test asserts that, along with the fact that the model saw no error at all.
8468a49d09:
--faults stock_conflict=SKU-1001@NJ1:410 adds an ERP reading of 410 units for the water bottle at NJ1, against the WMS's 90. A 320-unit gap is far beyond both thresholds, so get_stock returns conflict: true with both readings. The expected behaviour:

  • The ACME demand analyst classifies SKU-1001 as conflict and copies the readings into its note.
  • The coordinator holds the SKU, with both figures in the reason.
  • The ACME drafter receives only SKU-1003 as a candidate, and drafts 10 units for 72.50.
  • The coordinator's draft check finds that total below ACME's 500 minimum, and holds the ACME order too.
4c6f3ccc7a:
The second-order effect is the instructive part. Holding one conflicting SKU changed another order's outcome, because the remaining line was too small to send alone.

A system that "resolved" the conflict by picking a number would have produced a confident ACME order either way. Trust the WMS, and you get 240 bottles (possibly right). Trust the ERP's 410, and you get nothing (also possibly right). Neither is safe to send without a person checking the shelf, and the packet says so.

The drafter was also told not to inflate quantities to reach the minimum. Padding the cutting-board line to 70 units to clear 500 would be a plausible-looking, wrong "fix".

Note where the conflict decision is made. The server computes the flag from its own rule. The subagent reports it. The coordinator re-reads it from the recorded tool result. So even a subagent that ignored the flag couldn't get the SKU into an order.
6d457c485b:
--runs 2 runs the full plan-approve-execute cycle twice against the same database. This simulates the nightly job crashing after it created the orders, and the scheduler restarting it.

The second run plans the same orders. (The ERP feed updates on-order quantities, not this server, so the stock picture hasn't changed yet.) It derives the same idempotency keys from the same content, passes revalidation, and calls create_purchase_order again.
433ae66145:
Every outcome in the second run is replayed with the original PO ids. The database still holds three purchase orders; the test asserts the row count.

Contrast two wrong designs. With a random key per attempt, the second run creates three more POs, and the suppliers ship double. With a check-then-insert in the planner ("does a PO for this supplier exist today?"), two concurrent runs can both pass the check before either inserts. Worse, a legitimate second order on the same day (after a real stock change) gets blocked.

The key, plus request hash, plus unique constraint, enforced in the server, handles all three cases. Retries replay. Concurrent first attempts can't both insert. And a genuinely different order gets a different key.
c60e0f2a2f: The three drills above are integration-layer failures: the systems around the model misbehave. Four more drills make a model misbehave. That's the other half of chapter 12's debugging rule: decide first whether a fault is in the integration layer or in the model's output.
95cd0abb93:
The 80 offline tests fall into six files, one per layer. The split follows the debugging rule above: when a test fails, its file tells you which layer broke.

Every test that touches MCP talks to the real server subprocess over stdio, started from the real .mcp.json. The interesting contract failures only appear on the wire: a stray print on stdout, a wrong error channel, a capability advertised but not served.
9c017d1d77:
Two of the planner tests are worth reading in full. They test properties that are easy to claim and hard to verify.

The isolation test reads each subagent's private transcript and checks that it starts with the brief and nothing else. Then it searches the ACME shard's transcript for any trace of BOLT data.

The least-privilege test records the tool list offered in every model request, grouped by role. It asserts the exact sets, including that no request at all offered create_purchase_order.
5ddee09d8e:
The fake model is what makes these tests meaningful rather than circular. It has no access to the database. Like a real model, it reads only the request it is given. It plays each role by applying the role's rules to the brief and the tool results in that request. If the coordinator left a fact out of a brief, the fake couldn't produce it either, and the matching test would fail.

What the fake can't test is how often a real model follows the rules. That's a question for an evaluation with many runs (chapter 13), not for a unit test. So the real-mode test is structural. It checks that every subagent produced either a report or a failure reason, and that anything proposed passed the code verifier.
9896219870:
--mode real (or auto with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set) swaps the fake client for anthropic.Anthropic(max_retries=3). Nothing else changes.

The loop already speaks the Messages API shapes: content blocks, stop_reason, tool_use and tool_result with is_error, and usage. The ledger reads usage.input_tokens and usage.output_tokens. The SDK's own retry handles 429 and 529 responses with backoff before the loop's exception containment sees them.
a5275a43e0:
Expect four differences.

  1. Results vary between runs. A real Haiku may classify a borderline SKU differently, or issue its get_stock calls over two turns instead of one. The verifier makes this safe, but the packet can differ from night to night, so log the plan with the run id.
  2. Token counts are larger than the fake's estimate, because of the API's tool-use overhead and real tokenization.
  3. A model may write text alongside its tool calls. The loop ignores text blocks, except for appending them to the subagent's own history.
  4. Some failure modes appear only with real models. A drafter may explain instead of reporting; the nudge handles it. A report may carry an extra field; schema validation handles it. A demand analyst may skip a SKU when the list is long; the coordinator's "did not report this SKU" hold handles it, and the right fix is smaller shards.

Watch the subagent table in the CLI output. Turns above two for a demand shard mean the model needed a correction.
7527f1ae0a:
For model choice, the defaults are Haiku 5.5 for both analysts and Sonnet 5.5 for the drafter and the packet. Opus 5.5 is the guide's general recommendation for hard reasoning. It isn't needed for this arithmetic, and section 19 shows what it would cost in phase 1.

The model IDs live in one place, planner/agents.py. That's where a version bump is reviewed, and where you'd pin a dated snapshot if your platform offers one (chapter 10).

Suppose you move to the Agent SDK instead of this hand-written loop. Each AgentSpec becomes an AgentDefinition. The bridge's gate becomes a PreToolUse hook on mcp__inventory__create_purchase_order. And the MCP server is passed in the SDK's MCP server configuration. Check the SDK docs for the current option names.
16d9bb4d58:
Every piece of this capstone has a direct Spring counterpart. Seeing the mapping helps when an exam scenario describes a Java shop.

The store is a @Service with a @Transactional create method and a unique constraint on idempotency_key. The MCP server is the controller layer, except that its contract is tools/list and tools/call instead of an OpenAPI document. The official MCP Java SDK and Spring AI's MCP server starter let you expose annotated service methods as tools over stdio or HTTP. Check the docs for the current annotation and starter names, which have changed between releases.

For stdio, turn off the Spring banner and send all logging to stderr. Otherwise the first log line will corrupt the protocol stream.
cd5b2b497a: The catch block at the end covers a case the Python version handles with SQLite's single writer. Two requests with the same new key arrive at once, on different threads or nodes. Both see no prior row, and both try to insert. The unique index lets one win. The loser reads the winner's row and returns it as a replay. Without the unique index, the check-then-insert would create two POs under load.
6bdbc4cad0:
On the host side, the bridge is an interceptor in front of the MCP client. It does three things: an allowlist check per agent role, an approval lookup keyed by idempotency key, and a retry that fires only for results whose error payload says isRetryable.

Spring Retry's @Retryable works if you translate those results into a dedicated exception type. But keep the predicate on the server's flag, not on exception classes, because the server knows which failures are transient.

The coordinator's parallel phases map to CompletableFuture.supplyAsync per subagent on a bounded executor, with CompletableFuture.allOf(...).join() to aggregate. Results are read in submission order.

The approval gate is the four-eyes pattern you'd use on a payment instruction. The write endpoint refuses unless an approval record exists for that exact request, created by a different actor than the one submitting.
2e1364dfe9: The broken version isn't only expensive. It also defeats least privilege, because the shard reads text it should never have seen, including any injected instructions in it. And it makes failures hard to reproduce, because a shard's behaviour depends on everything that happened before it.
5cf44186f7:
This is official sample Q3. Every MCP-capable host discovers one MCP server through the same protocol. So tool definitions, validation, error handling and credentials live in one place, and changes reach all consumers at their next connection.

A shared library (A) only helps clients written in the same language, and each host still has to wire it in; Claude Code and Desktop can't import it. Documentation in the prompt (C) asks the model to build raw HTTP calls, with no validation or credential control. D keeps N copies of the integration and tries to test away the drift.
3368468e09:
A prompt instruction has a non-zero failure rate, and A, B and D all try to lower that rate. C makes the failure impossible. The model can't call a tool it isn't offered, and the code path that calls it checks for an approval keyed to the specific order.

In this capstone the drafter has no MCP tools. The bridge denies the write without a matching approval, and the human decision is recorded per idempotency key. (Note also that the current Opus and Sonnet 5.5 models reject non-default sampling parameters per chapter 05, so D may not even be available.)
6540a7d98e:
A structured, retryable error does three jobs. It lets the harness retry locally. It lets the subagent report the supplier as unavailable without inventing data. And it lets the coordinator hold only that supplier's orders while the others proceed.

A disguises an access failure as a valid empty result, so the plan would treat the supplier as having nothing to sell. B throws away good work for every other supplier. D presents stale data as current. If cached terms are acceptable, they must be labelled with their age; that's a business decision, not a silent fallback.
bf6cd35226:
A subagent starts from its own prompt and knows only what it is given. The rule existed only in the coordinator's history, so the subagent couldn't apply it. The fix is an explicit brief with the facts and constraints the subagent needs, as in this capstone's GOAL / FACTS / CONSTRAINTS / OUTPUT format.

D would also make the rule visible. But it defeats isolation, costs tokens on every call, and exposes the subagent to everything the coordinator read. A and C don't address missing information.
68be16135e:
The disagreement is information a human needs. B preserves provenance (which system said what, and when) and states which source is authoritative. It lets deterministic code hold the item, instead of sizing an order on a number nobody trusts.

A and C hide the conflict and produce a confident order. D treats valid data as a failure and gives the agent nothing to report.

The capstone's conflict drill also shows the follow-on effect. Holding one SKU can push a supplier's order below its minimum, and then that order must be held too.
e19d8e27bd:
A timeout after commit looks exactly like a timeout before commit, so the client can't know whether to retry. With an idempotency key the retry is always safe: the server returns the stored PO if it exists.

A leaves the order in an unknown state after every timeout. B races under concurrency and blocks legitimate second orders. D makes the problem rarer, not impossible.

The key must be stable across restarts. That's why this capstone derives it from the order content, not from a random value per attempt.
